seo.title: Halal Food in Seoul, Neighbourhood by Neighbourhood
seo.description: Where certified halal restaurants actually are in Seoul, the Itaewon mosque, and what to avoid at a convenience store.

title: Halal food in Seoul, neighbourhood by neighbourhood
intro: I've driven enough Indonesian and Malaysian families around Seoul to know that the sightseeing is never the hard part of the trip. Lunch is. Here's what I've actually learned, not a copied list.

blocks.text: Itaewon is the anchor, not the whole answer

Seoul Central Mosque sits on the hill above the main Itaewon strip, open to visitors outside prayer times, with a women's section upstairs. The street below it is the real halal cluster — Turkish, Pakistani, Uzbek, and one Korean restaurant doing halal bulgogi that surprises people. If you only eat halal food in one part of Seoul, this is the part.
The mistake is thinking Itaewon means you're covered for the whole trip. It's a fifteen-minute drive from most hotels, not somewhere you loop back to for every meal.

There's a small prayer room near the shopping streets, and a handful of street stalls carry halal certification — but not every cart with a sign does. I point out which ones before guests queue, because by the time you're holding food it's too late to ask. Some of the bigger department stores also run halal-certified counters in their basement food halls, which is worth knowing if the weather turns.

items: Look for the actual certification mark, not just an Arabic-script sign
"Muslim-friendly" often just means no pork — alcohol may still be served
Basement food halls in major department stores sometimes have certified counters
Ask before you queue, not after you're holding the tray

blocks.text: What to actually avoid at a convenience store

Convenience stores are everywhere and genuinely useful for snacks and drinks, but gelatin turns up in things you wouldn't expect — gummies, some yogurts, certain instant noodle seasoning packets. If you're strict, checking ingredient lists here matters more than at a sit-down restaurant, where at least someone can answer a direct question.
During Ramadan, the day looks different

A later start, sightseeing in the cooler hours, and being seated at a restaurant before Maghrib rather than scrambling after. Tell your driver you're fasting and a decent one will plan the stops around it rather than around the usual tourist schedule.

Pair the mosque and Itaewon lunch with the palace and Myeongdong in the same loop rather than treating food as a separate errand — it's exactly how the Seoul day tour is routed, prayer times and all.
